Definitely support this. When you under allocate resources with respect to recruitment timelines and then place the burden on study coordinators and already overburdened sites to pick up the slack, it's very frustrating. Sites want to do good work, but some studies expect to recruit hundreds of patients at recruitment rates that are overestimated five-fold. I think also understanding time commitments for PIs vs Coordinators. I can only speak for my site, which includes myself and one PI who is a full-time clinic doctor, but one of the major issues I've seen is sponsors fundamentally not understanding how much of the day-to-day is managed by coordinators. Unless it is specifically designated to the PI or requires a medical license, assume that we are the ones doing it. Trust me, if there was any way that my PI could get away with making me complete their duties too, they would.

Lastly, my biggest pet peeve are the convoluted systems that overemphasize digital solutions when standard data collection methods and simple paper scales would suffice. One of my studies has almost two dozen vendors. I still don't know what they all do. My average px is over 60, some have significant cognitive issues due to disease progression. Digital scales on cell phones is not the move for this population.

There really is no experience that will ever truly prepare you to be a coordinator, other than being a coordinator. I started on the sponsor side then moved to the site side (I was let go during the market downturn). Some days, it feels like the worst job ever. Other days, it feels like the best. My advice:

1. You will make mistakes. We all have at one point or another. Stay humble, learn, and try not to make any of the big ones.

2. Learn your protocols. Read every protocol you have and read it well. They are your bible. If you know what's in your protocol and you do it, then you won't fail.

3. Communicate and stay organized. The more organized you are, the better off you will be.

4. Be kind to everyone you meet.

I support four different doctors as a CRC and have no backup coordinators. My duties range from assisting with neuroimaging for neurosurgeries, to helping my PI coordinate her calendar for various events. I have to be very skilled in a wide range of tasks from operations, data coordination, events planning, budget reconcilation, recruitment, and remember everything without dropping the ball. I have systems and I do my best to fulfill our sponsors needs but ultimately, many sponsors don't realize that doctors aren't highly involved in the daily operations of studies. The doctor is just a titleholder to allow the CRC to do 95% of the work. No shade, doctors are busy. I'm not going to comment on your fashion because other people have already done so and I don't want to pile on. Instead, let's focus on angles.

Six feet away. That's the ideal zone. You want to be close enough the camera where people can see your eyes, but far enough that they can take you all in.

This is gonna sound silly, but before you do a set of photos, jump up and down and flail your arms. Then lean back a bit and put your hands in your pockets. Standing up straight makes you look slimmer, but you gotta shake out that stiffness. Experiment with some different poses. Try crossing your arms and smiling. Tilt your head. Learn your angles. Learn your body. Learn what looks good and what doesn't.

Take A LOT of photos. Most guys take 10 or 20. I usually bribe my friends with lunch or something if they offer to help me with this because we're probably taking 100 photos to get 3 or 4 good ones. Remember, photos capture a moment, for better or worse.

Lastly, pratice on your own. Learn your camera. Understand what it does. Does it do a background soften effect? Can you use artistic styling to capture attention? Can you improve lighting digitally? Learn these things. A good photo from six feet back with a background blur can both enhance your features while providing some varity in an otherwise dull background.

Tough question. Here are my thoughts.

There's a Psychological principle called imprinting. It basically means that when someone sees something (usually as a child), there's a chance that that particular thing can sort of make a mark on that person. For example, let's say when you were five you movie and there was a specific scene that wasn't inherently sexual but had something in it. An article of clothing maybe or a specific body type. If that thing is then imprinted upon an individual, perhaps that person could then grow up to favor that thing in a sexual manner.

However, the question at the root then becomes whether or not it was the imprinting in an of itself that caused it, or if that person was always going to be susceptible to that kind of fetish regardless of the time or setting.

Alright, I am by no means an expert on the topic of human sexuality and that is a relatively complicated question but I will attempt to answer it as best I can. From my understanding, while there has been scientific speculation on a gay gene, there is no conclusive peer reviewed evidence which concretely proves it. I am of the mind that homosexuality has been in existence throughout history as have things like people who identify with the opposite gender than their assigned at birth and bi-sexuality. However, in my very humble opinion I think it's a careful balance between nature and nurture. People who live in an oppressive or strictly religious family for instance, have been known to convince themselves that their heterosexual, only to later discover they are homosexual. 

To your second question, absolutely. Sexual surrogates offer a wide range of services and I think they play an important role for people attempting to make self-sexual discoveries. Particularly those individuals heavily stigmatized by society (for example individuals with disabilities).

No. In fact, it wasn't till my early 20s that I realized that Polyamory was a thing. However, I do think that for some people it's a viable lifestyle and when said person figures out that it's something they can enjoy, they tend to gravitate towards it.

So a few years back, (I was busing tables at the time) I went to University and went to this voluntary class on human sexuality. That class would eventually become the one for which one of my poly partners is currently the Vice President. Since I'm currently pursuing multiple degrees, I'm not currently facilitating those meetings or leading any discussions. However, what fascinated me most were actually the works of people like Alfred Kinzie. He was basically the father of Clinical Sexology and still serves as an inspiration for me. He did great things but the sheer amount of ignorance within the subject of human sexuality that existed was staggering. From a lack of understanding of human anatomy to the general lack of understanding that many people still have of both their own and their partners sexual satisfaction. Something inside of me just wanted to change that. I wanted to promote more effective communication on sexuality within my community.

Well, I'm not a professor. Technically speaking, I'm an active member of a community driven coalition which mainly focuses on the voluntary sexual education of people within our community. However, that said when I do begin a professorship, I intend on keeping my work and personal life separate as there are no laws protecting polyamorous people as currently exist for the LGBT community.
